text: Pandora: A Person Created Only to Punish Others
Many people remember Pandora opening a box.

Disease, toil, and every kind of calamity flew out, leaving only hope inside. The story is therefore often told as a warning about curiosity: because a woman could not resist opening something she should not have opened, humanity has suffered ever since.
But in the early account preserved by Hesiod, the container is a jar. More importantly, the story really begins not with Pandora’s curiosity, but with the struggle between Zeus and Prometheus.
Prometheus brought fire back to humanity. Zeus decided to make humans pay for it.
He ordered the gods to create a woman.

She had human form and a human voice, learned weaving, received beauty and allure, and was also endowed with deceptive speech and an insatiable heart. She was named, adorned, and then sent to Epimetheus as a “gift.”
Before she had even entered human life, others had already written down what she was for.
She was created to punish other people.
This makes Pandora very different from the villains of many stories.
Villains usually have desires of their own first, then choose to fulfill them by harming others. We can examine their motives, judgment, and responsibility.
Pandora, however, first appears within someone else’s plan.

Others shape her body, allocate her abilities, give her a name, and decide where she will go. She is sent among humans not because she has chosen a particular life, but because Zeus means to use her to answer Prometheus and humanity.
The story even calls this arrangement a gift.
That is precisely its sharpest point.

A gift is ordinarily supposed to bring something to its recipient. But the true purpose of Pandora as a “gift” belongs to the giver from the outset. She is not sent to fulfill a life of her own, nor to answer the recipient’s needs. She is placed in a conflict that began before she appeared, becoming one side’s way of striking the other.
When a person is arranged in this way, they may possess many abilities, yet not one of them serves to decide why they exist.
Being able to speak does not mean being able to define one’s own questions.
Being able to act does not mean being able to choose what one’s actions serve.
Being given beauty, skills, and the power to influence others does not mean being given a direction of one’s own.
Everything Pandora possesses has already been incorporated into the use others have assigned her.
This does not mean that everything Pandora later does is beyond judgment.
In Works and Days, she opens the jar and lets its calamities scatter among humans. Having one’s circumstances arranged by others does not automatically remove responsibility from every action.
But responsibility needs to be distinguished at different levels.
Who designed the whole plan?
Who manufactured this “gift” for revenge?
Who decided to send her to humanity?
Who knew what she had been endowed with, and how much did the person receiving her know?
What did she herself know about her origins and purpose?
The text does not answer all these questions.
But it at least prevents us from reducing the entire disaster to: “She should not have opened that container.”

If a person has been deliberately made, trained, and placed in a certain position to produce a certain outcome, responsibility for what actually happens afterward cannot fall solely on the hand closest to the consequences.
The designer does not disappear from the story simply because he did not open the jar himself.
Likewise, the person who carries out the act does not become an object with no position from which to act merely because others once designed her.
That is precisely the difficulty: a person can be both a means within someone else’s plan and someone who actually acts.
Acknowledging only the former writes her as an implement without any existence of her own.
Acknowledging only the latter hides all those who made her and prescribed her purpose behind the scenes.
Later tellings often supply Pandora with an explanation very familiar to us: a woman brings trouble through curiosity.
This explanation is exceedingly convenient.

It turns a story about power, revenge, and making a person into a story about an individual flaw of character. A punishment originally designed by the highest power ends up seeming to result merely from one person’s failure to control herself.
Moreover, this explanation puts Pandora to use twice.
First, inside the story, she is used as a way to punish humanity.
Second, outside the story, she is used as an example proving that a certain kind of person is dangerous, weak, or untrustworthy.
Not only does she have no purpose of her own; even her reason for bringing disaster has been prepared for her by later generations.
But the early text does not give us enough material to explain in detail what she was thinking when she opened the jar.
We do not know whether she knew what was inside, whether she understood why she had been sent, or whether she could have refused the role the gods had arranged for her.
This silence matters.
Faced with a character whose inner life has not been fully written, there are two mistakes especially easy to make.
One is to condemn her outright as the source of malice.
The other is to restore her dignity by writing in a modern story of resistance that the text never supplies.
Both speak for her.
The more honest approach is to acknowledge that the story gives her insufficient room to speak, while recognizing what that absence itself means.
Being shaped by others is not a condition unique to Pandora.

No one grows up from a complete blank. Our language, abilities, habits, and many of our desires come from environments we did not choose. Others teach us how to live and inevitably influence, to some degree, who we want to become.
So the question cannot be whether a person has ever been shaped by others.
The real question is whether that shaping leaves them the possibility of reinterpreting and changing the uses they have been assigned.
A child can be taught a skill and later use it somewhere their parents never anticipated.
Someone can enter a role and then discover that its aims are not ones they wish to take on for the long term.
Even a tool originally made for one purpose may be redirected by its user toward a new problem.
As long as a person can still turn back and ask, “Is this really what I want to do?”, abilities supplied from outside need not imprison them forever.
Pandora’s tragedy is that Hesiod’s account scarcely opens this dimension for her.

She is created with a purpose already attached; she enters the human world with that purpose; her actions are used to fulfill it; finally, she is remembered as the entrance through which human suffering came into the world.
From beginning to end, she is surrounded by a struggle belonging to others.
The story also confronts us with a harder question.
Suppose a person really does receive life, abilities, and form from a creator. Does that give the creator the authority to decide what that person should live for?
Giving something often produces an illusion of ownership.
I gave you this opportunity, so you should use it according to my plan.
I developed your abilities, so your future should prove my judgment right.
I created the conditions in which you can now live, so I am better entitled than you to explain what your life is for.
But “Without what I gave you, you would not be as you are now” is not the same statement as “Therefore you should become what I specify.”
An origin can explain where an ability comes from, but cannot automatically own every later use of it.
A kindness can call forth gratitude, but cannot turn the recipient’s future into property owed in return.
Still less can creation inherently amount to ownership.

Of course, Pandora’s story does not make this judgment for us. The order of gods and humans in which it belongs takes the gods’ arrangements for humanity as part of the world. Nor does Pandora step forward to declare that she rejects her origins.
This is an ancient account that conflicts with our judgments today, not a fable that secretly endorsed modern answers all along.
Its value lies precisely in its unvarnished portrayal of another world: a being with human form, voice, and capacity for action can be understood entirely as a means within other people’s conflict.
We need not pretend that resistance to this arrangement is already hidden deep within the story.
We need only take its cost seriously.
After Pandora opens the jar, calamities enter the human world.
But before the jar is opened, something else has already happened.
A person has first been placed inside other people’s purposes.
She has been made, named, adorned, and sent away, without being asked where she wants to place the life she has received.
So perhaps what this story leaves us is not only a container full of calamities.
It also leaves us a person who was scarcely allowed to speak.
When a story tells us only what she was used for, without letting us know what matters to her herself, what is lost is more than a passage describing a character’s psychology.
What is lost is this possibility:
Even if a person receives their form, abilities, and name from others, they remain more than the use others assign them.
Pandora was created as a gift to be sent into the human world.
But a true gift should one day leave the giver’s purpose behind.
She was never allowed to leave.

*Textual basis and note on versions: this essay draws primarily on Hesiod’s Works and Days, lines 42–105, with Theogony, lines 535–616, as a comparison. The container in the early text is a jar, not the “box” of later popular retellings. The two works do not place exactly the same emphasis on the account of the first woman. This essay neither combines them into an undifferentiated version nor invents modern answers for the inner life of Pandora that the text leaves unwritten.*
